questions_asked:
# Expert Question 1 (structural)

In a busy US airport security checkpoint, which single step do passengers
typically complain about the most, and why?

# Expert Question 2 (parameter, building on exchange 1)

You said passengers complain most about removing and repacking belongings at
the X-ray belt. How many seconds does a typical passenger actually spend at
the belt doing all of that?

# Expert Question 3 (edge case / variance driver, building on exchanges 1-2)

Even at airports with normally short waits, lines sometimes balloon suddenly
with no obvious cause. What actually triggers those surprise surges in
practice?

# Expert Question 4 (parameter for the outlier mechanism from exchange 3)

You said one flagged or slow passenger can block a lane for minutes. In a
normal day, what fraction of passengers actually gets pulled aside for extra
search?

# Expert Question 5 (cultural norms, for subproblem c; building on earlier exchanges)

Different nationalities move through the same security belt quite differently
in practice. What differences do you actually notice?

# Expert Question 6 (boundary behavior during a lane outage; building on exchange 3)

When one lane shuts down mid-bank, what actually happens to the people
already in its line?

# Expert Question 7 (structural: queue geometry; building on exchange 6)

At a busy checkpoint, do travelers pick a specific lane's line to join, or do
they first stand in one shared line that feeds all open lanes?

# Expert Question 8 (staffing norm during peak; building on exchanges 3 and 7)

When a bank of flights arrives and the shared line starts growing, how quickly
do TSA supervisors usually open extra lanes, and what triggers it?

# Expert Question 9 (validating a key model assumption; building on exchange 2)

Pre-Check travelers skip shoes, belts, jackets and laptop removal. From what
you have seen, does that actually make their belt step noticeably faster than
regular passengers' — and by how much, roughly?

# Expert Question 10 (policy lever; building on exchange 5)

Some airports now put bin and divest tables before the queue, so people empty
belongings while still waiting. In your experience, does that genuinely speed
things up, or does it backfire?
expert_answers:
The step passengers complain about most is the divestiture/reclaim step in Zone B/C — removing shoes, belts, jackets, laptops, and liquids, placing them in bins, and then waiting at the far end of the X-ray belt to collect belongings.

Why: it is the step where passengers are personally and physically involved, it is slow and awkward (unbuckling, repacking, separating electronics), and it is where the queue visibly stalls. It also carries the highest anxiety — the fear of losing or having items taken — and the reclaim wait is unpredictable because bin exit times vary with X-ray flags and secondary searches. ID check and the scanner itself are brief and passive by comparison, so complaints concentrate on the belt.

A typical passenger spends roughly 30–60 seconds at the belt for the divest/reclaim cycle: about 15–30 seconds to divest (remove shoes, belt, jacket, laptop, liquids, load bins) and about 15–30 seconds to reclaim and repack on the far side. Frequent/Pre-Check travelers with little to divest run closer to 10–20 seconds total; inexperienced or heavily laden travelers (families, multiple bins, flagged bags) can take 60–90 seconds or more. This is an empirical judgment from observed checkpoint behavior, not a precise measured figure.

The dominant trigger is a **temporary loss of parallel capacity**, not a surge in arrivals. Concretely:

- **Lane closures / staffing gaps**: a screener goes on break, is pulled to another lane, or a lane is shut for a shift change. With 3–4 lanes open, losing one cuts throughput ~25–33% instantly while arrivals continue unchanged — the queue grows fast and visibly.
- **A single slow or flagged passenger**: one pat-down, one bag pulled for secondary search, or one traveler with many bins can block a lane for 1–3 minutes. At low-traffic hours there is no slack to absorb it, so a handful of such events in sequence produces a sudden line.
- **Equipment stoppage**: X-ray or millimeter-wave unit fault, belt jam, or recalibration takes a lane out entirely.
- **Arrival bunching**: banks of flights landing/departing together, or a delayed flight dumping its passengers into the checkpoint at once.
- **Divestiture clustering**: a family or group with many bins, or an inexperienced traveler, stalls the belt and backs up the whole lane.

The key point: at normally-short-wait airports, utilization is low but **buffer staffing is thin**, so variance comes from capacity drops and service-time outliers, not demand spikes.

Roughly 2–5% of passengers are pulled aside for extra screening on a normal day — this covers both bag flags (secondary bag search at X-ray) and passenger flags (pat-down after the scanner or metal detector). Pre-Check passengers are at the low end, near 1–2%; regular-lane passengers run higher, around 3–6%, because they divest more and carry more items that trigger alarms.

The rate is not uniform: it clusters by traveler type and by hour. Families, infrequent travelers, and passengers with liquids/electronics packed ambiguously flag more often, so during a bank of leisure flights the effective pull-aside rate in a given lane can momentarily run well above the daily average.

This is an empirical judgment from observed checkpoint behavior, not a precise measured figure.

The most consistent real-world differences I notice at the belt:

- **Personal-space norms (US/Northern Europe)**: travelers leave a visible gap to the person ahead, won't close up even when the queue is long, and won't reach past or around others. This wastes belt length and slows the effective service rate at high load.
- **Collective-efficiency norms (Swiss/German/Nordic)**: people self-organize — pre-divest before reaching the belt, stack bins neatly, move off promptly to reclaim. Lower variance, but they will also wait their turn rather than assert position.
- **Individual-efficiency norms (Chinese, and to a degree Indian/Middle Eastern urban travelers)**: travelers edge forward, fill gaps, and start divesting early; throughput per lane is higher but reclaim is more chaotic and "cutting" complaints rise.
- **Group/family travelers (any culture)**: move as a unit, occupy the belt longer, and block others regardless of nationality.
- **Infrequent vs. frequent travelers**: this often dominates nationality — a frequent Chinese flyer and a frequent American behave more alike than either does to a first-time flyer of their own culture.

Net: culture mainly shifts **spacing discipline, pre-divestiture timing, and queue-position assertiveness**, which change both mean service time and its variance.

When a lane shuts down mid-bank, the people already in that line are almost never simply abandoned. In practice:

- **They are merged into the adjacent open lane(s)**, usually at the front or by having them re-form at the back of the neighboring queue. The common real-world choice is to let the already-waiting passengers go first (or interleave), because leaving them stranded triggers complaints and perceived unfairness.
- **The merge itself costs throughput**: the receiving lane briefly stalls while people shuffle over, re-establish position, and re-divest. Expect a short disruption of roughly 30–90 seconds per merge event, plus a temporary dip in that lane's service rate.
- **Positional conflict is the main friction**: this is exactly where "cutting" disputes arise, and where cultural norms matter — travelers with strong personal-space/queue-order norms (US, Northern Europe) re-form orderly and lose time; individual-efficiency travelers fill the gap immediately.
- **If no adjacent lane can absorb them** (all lanes near capacity), the line simply grows in place until the lane reopens; passengers wait, and the queue length spikes.

Net effect: a lane outage does not just remove capacity — it adds a transient merge penalty and a variance spike on the surviving lanes.

At busy US checkpoints, the standard geometry is a **single shared feeder queue** (Zone A/B), not per-lane lines. Passengers first queue for ID check, then join one common serpentine line that feeds all open screening lanes; a staff member directs each passenger to the next available lane as it frees up.

Per-lane lines do exist, but mainly at smaller or low-traffic checkpoints, or when lanes are physically separated (e.g., a distinct Pre-Check lane). Even then, travelers often self-select into the shortest visible line rather than being assigned.

The distinction matters for your model: with a shared feeder queue, a lane outage does **not** strand a dedicated line of people — it just reduces the number of servers draining the common queue, so the queue grows in place. The "merge penalty" from exchange 6 applies mainly to the per-lane-line configuration, or to the moment staff redirect the shared queue.

Extra lanes are opened **reactively, not preemptively**, and the lag is typically **several minutes — on the order of 5–15 minutes** from the moment the queue visibly grows to the moment an added lane is actually screening.

What triggers it:
- **Visual queue length / line crossing a physical threshold** (the line reaching a rope, a doorway, or spilling into the concourse) — this is the dominant trigger, not a forecast of arriving flights.
- **Passenger complaints or a supervisor's walk-by observation.**
- **Scheduled shift/break timing** — lanes are often added when a break rotation ends rather than when demand peaks.

Why the lag: opening a lane is not instant. It requires a free officer (pulled from another lane, a break, or a non-screening duty), a supervisor's decision, and a few minutes to set up and reach steady service rate. So the system responds to the *symptom* (a long line) after it has already formed, which is exactly why queues overshoot and then drain — a major source of the variance described in exchange 3.

This is an empirical judgment from observed checkpoint operations, not a precise measured figure.

Yes — noticeably faster, and the gap is real but not dramatic.

Roughly: Pre-Check divest/reclaim runs about **10–20 seconds** versus **30–60 seconds** for regular passengers — so the belt step is roughly **2–3× faster**, saving on the order of **20–40 seconds per passenger**. The saving comes almost entirely from the divest side (no shoe/belt/jacket removal, laptop stays in bag, fewer bins), not from reclaim.

Two caveats that matter for your model:
- The gap **shrinks when Pre-Check passengers still have liquids/electronics to pull out**, or when they are infrequent travelers who fumble regardless of rules.
- Pre-Check's real advantage is often **lower variance**, not just lower mean — fewer bins and fewer alarms mean fewer belt stalls.

Empirical judgment from observed checkpoint behavior, not a measured figure.

It genuinely helps, with conditions.

It works when the pre-queue divest area is **sized to the queue and staffed/laid out so people actually use it** — travelers then arrive at the belt already divested, cutting belt occupancy toward the Pre-Check-like 10–20 seconds and, more importantly, cutting its variance (fewer bins, fewer fumbles, fewer stalls). The gain is largest for infrequent travelers and families, who are the main belt-stallers.

It backfires when:
- **The table is too small or too far from the belt**, so people divest twice or carry loose items forward anyway.
- **Passengers won't divest early** because they fear losing sight of belongings or being rushed — common with strong personal-space/queue-order norms (US, Northern Europe), where people wait until their turn.
- **It just relocates the bottleneck**: divestiture moves into the queue, so the queue itself slows and the shared feeder line grows, without net throughput gain if belt capacity wasn't the binding constraint.

Net: it converts belt time into queue time and mainly buys **variance reduction**, not raw throughput, unless the belt was the constraint.
